thread.title: UMich community reacts to launch of Year of Life-Changing Education
thread.title_full: UMich community reacts to launch of Year of Life-Changing Education

author: Alyssa Tisch
title: UMich community reacts to launch of Year of Life-Changing Education
text:
The University of Michigan announced its 2025-2026 theme, Year of Life-Changing Education, Aug. 25. The theme is part of the University’s Look to Michigan vision, made up of five core impact areas: Life-Changing Education; Human Health and Well-Being; Democracy, Civic and Global Engagement; Energy, Climate Action, Sustainability and Environmental Equity; and Advanced Technology. Each area will get its own year of focus. This follows last year’s theme of the Year of Democracy, Civic Empowerment and Global Engagement.
The Year of Life-Changing Education has four goals for improving the future of education: fostering open inquiry and productive disagreements; expanding pathways and access across Michigan; marking the past and co-creating the campus and education of the future; and sharing scholarship, shaping solutions.
In an email to The Michigan Daily, Angela Dillard, vice provost for undergraduate education and co-chair for the Year of Life-Changing Education, described the potential implementation of each goal. Dillard wrote the Talking Maize & Blue app-based course and Open Inquiry week of events support the University’s goal of fostering productive dialogue on campus.
“Fostering Open Inquiry and Productive Disagreements includes the Talking Maize & Blue app-based course that we designed for first-year students, and which over 80% have completed,” Dillard wrote. “It also includes the upcoming Open Inquiry Week that will feature a public conversation that I’ll be moderating with Glenn Loury. We’ll be demonstrating ways to dialogue across differences, pursue ideas with curiosity and courage, practicing and learning from disagreements.”
Dillard wrote she is also excited about Campus of the Future, a design competition for students to share their ideas for a future U-M campus. Dillard explained this idea came from a previous course and competition.
“This is still in the planning stages, but the idea is to revive an older version that happened around a course in 2015 and a design competition in 2017 as part of the U-M Bicentennial Theme Year,” Dillard wrote. “We want to find, celebrate and adopt as many innovative ideas as possible and listen to and be inspired by students in the process.”
In an interview with The Daily, Public Policy Professor Sarah Cohodes said initiatives that help more low-income students attend the University, which are described in the University’s plans regarding expanding access, will have a significant impact.
“For me, the focus on access is the most important and powerful, because that’s where you change the experiences of individuals,” Cohodes said. “Access to the (University) can make a big difference in terms of where their life trajectory is going to go.”
Recently, President Donald Trump’s administration has taken several actions targeting higher education, including influencing policy through funding threats, cutting funding for some schools and setting restrictions on international students. LSA sophomore Tyler Layman, told The Daily she felt the education theme came at a good time, considering the actions of the current administration.
“I think this theme is really important and almost at a critical time, especially with the current administration doing a lot of controversial things in the realm of education,” Layman said. “I think it’s really admirable that they’re deciding that this year, we want our focus on education.”
In an interview with The Daily, Rackham student Megan Connors said the theme was well-timed in promoting educational progress, especially as a recent study ranked the state of Michigan 44th in the nation in education.
“We’re not making as much progress as a lot of people had hoped for in terms of closing achievement gaps,” Connors said. “The (COVID-19) pandemic had a really big negative impact that we haven’t yet figured out how to rebound from. But I think there were other factors — even pre-pandemic, notably like the influence of technology — that were already having an impact that we haven’t quite solved.”
Connors also said she is curious to see how much attention this theme will receive amongst students.
“I’ll just be curious to see how many people actually know about this initiative, and what types of events it looks like,” Connors said. “I hope it’s broadly participated in.”
LSA senior Isabella Liu, executive director of Opportunities to Educate Children, told The Daily she was skeptical that the University will take significant steps toward its goals but hopes the year’s theme and projects will be successful.
“I think that as an institution, there’s a lot of opportunity for us to be active and have a direct impact on our community,” Liu said. “I don’t know that we have always been able to follow through on these opportunities as (the University). The University has critics and I don’t think the criticism is always misplaced. I’m really hoping that the Year of Life-Changing Education can live up to what it sets out to do, and really has a tangible impact because education can actually be life-changing.”
In an interview with The Daily, Education junior Jane Atkins, co-president of Future Educators, said she hopes to see the University take actions that impact students directly.
“I feel like what we’re really looking for is for the University to hold themselves accountable to these statements that they’re making in this theme year,” Atkins said. “I hope that students can see the actionable items that they will be taking and that it will impact them and we can see real results from these promises that they’re making.”
